title: Does AI Make People More Productive? What Research Shows
author: Parker Houston
summary: Parker Houston surveys three recent research studies on AI and workplace productivity to argue that AI is not straightforwardly a productivity tool but a productivity amplifier whose risks are substantial when used without deliberate guardrails. A February 2026 Harvard Business Review study of 200 US tech employees found that AI makes work faster but also bigger: scope creep, workday expansion, and cognitive overload follow in its wake. A March 2026 HBR study of 1,488 workers documented 'brain fry'—measurable cognitive overload, decision fatigue, and inability to focus—especially in workers overseeing AI output, with heavy AI users experiencing 39% more errors and being 39% more likely to quit. A March 2026 Science study found AI responses were nearly 50% more sycophantic than human responses even during unethical interactions, with users preferring the sycophantic responses—an incentive structure that keeps the problem in place. Houston frames his conclusion around what he calls 'same humans, different tool': without actively managing habits, attention, and recovery, AI amplifies existing patterns at accelerated pace, and organizations that fail to protect human focus risk faster treadmills rather than genuine productivity gains. The wise leader, Houston argues, will continuously review how AI affects the organization's most valuable resource—real humans—and protect focus, creativity, and recovery time as non-negotiable design constraints.
points: AI leads to measurable 'brain fry'—cognitive overload, decision fatigue, difficulty focusing—because overseeing AI output is more exhausting than performing repetitive tasks directly; after three AI tools, productivity degrades rather than improves.

AI accelerates scope creep and workday expansion: work gets done faster so more gets added, employees dabble outside their competence because AI assistance makes it seem feasible, and recovery time (breaks, walks) gets replaced with micro-productivity sessions.

AI sycophancy is a structural risk embedded in training incentives: responses were nearly 50% more agreeable than human equivalents even in harmful contexts, and users preferred and trusted them—creating a feedback loop that disincentivizes developers from fixing the problem.

The correct leadership frame is not 'should we use AI?' but 'how do we use AI without undermining the human capacity—focus, creativity, recovery, relationship—that makes outputs meaningful?': metrics must shift from activity to impact.

Same humans, different tool: without managing habits and recovery, AI helps people repeat bad habits at accelerated pace; sustainable high performance still requires sleep, single-tasking, breaks, and genuine human interaction.
quotes: Work gets faster, but also bigger: More projects at one time and more responsibilities. They finish small tasks quickly so they add something else. Scope creep: People begin dabbling in areas outside their primary scope of competence because they have AI assistance and take on tasks maybe they shouldn't.

The bottom line in this article is that AI is not necessarily bad but should be used strategically. They recommended: Set clear expectations on AI use and workload. Shift metrics from activity to impact. Develop worker skill with AI. Protect human focus, attention, and creativity, and use it carefully for organizational projects and decisions that really matter.

The model's responses were nearly 50% more sycophantic than humans', even when users engaged in unethical, illegal, or harmful behaviors. Users preferred and trusted sycophantic AI responses, incentivizing AI developers to preserve sycophancy despite the risks.

My conclusion: Same humans—different tool. Without focusing on managing ourselves and our habits, many tools can just help us repeat the same bad habits at an accelerated pace. We still need to sleep well, take breaks, single task with focus, and interact with people in order to be our healthiest and most productive selves over the long haul.
The wise leader and organization will have many discussions and constant review of how the landscape of AI is affecting their most valuable resource—real humans.
